ai.title: Medical Microbiology Overview
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A clinician‑focused guide to the microbes most relevant in East African low‑resource hospitals, linking transmission, disease patterns, bedside diagnosis and pragmatic management.

b: Focus on organisms that are common, severe, or have public‑health impact.
Emphasise bedside clues when labs are unavailable.
sections.p: Medical microbiology studies bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites that cause human disease. In low‑resource settings the burden is shaped by HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B, sickle‑cell disease and limited laboratory capacity.

b: Gram‑positive cocci: Staphylococcus aureus (catalase+, coagulase+), Streptococcus pneumoniae (alpha‑hemolytic).
Gram‑negative rods: Escherichia coli (lactose fermenter), Klebsiella pneumoniae (mucoid colonies).
Acid‑fast bacilli: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (slow growth, cord formation).
Protozoa: Plasmodium falciparum (ring forms, gametocytes).
sections.p: Key microbial groups are described by Gram stain, shape, growth requirements and virulence factors that explain clinical patterns.

b: Fecal‑oral: Shigella, cholera, Giardia – contaminated water/food.
Respiratory droplets: TB, influenza, SARS‑CoV‑2 – close contact.
Vector‑borne: Plasmodium – Anopheles mosquito; Leishmania – sandfly.
Sexual: HIV, hepatitis B – blood or mucosal exposure.
sections.p: Understanding how microbes reach the patient guides prevention and history taking.

b: Pneumonia: S. pneumoniae (community‑acquired), K. pneumoniae (post‑influenza, HIV).
Septicemia: NTS (non‑typhoidal Salmonella) in sickle‑cell disease; S. aureus in skin breaks.
Meningitis: N. meningitidis (young adults), Cryptococcus neoformans (advanced HIV).
Diarrhoea: ETEC, Shigella, Giardia – especially in children and malnourished.
sections.p: Clinically important syndromes are grouped by organ system, severity and typical patient risk factors.
Prioritise bedside assessment, simple bedside tests and the most informative laboratory investigations that are often available.

t.a: Gram stain of pus or CSF
t.b: Identifies bacterial morphology and guides empiric therapy; Gram‑positive cocci in clusters suggest S. aureus.
Answers whether Plasmodium is present; a positive result mandates antimalarial treatment.
Detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance; if unavailable, use sputum smear microscopy and clinical scoring.
Screens for urinary tract infection when culture is not feasible.

b: First‑line antibiotics: ampicillin‑gentamicin for neonatal sepsis; ceftriaxone for severe pneumonia when Gram‑negative rods suspected.
Avoid fluoroquinolones in children and pregnant women due to cartilage toxicity.
Antimalarial: artemisinin‑based combination therapy (ACT) – chosen for rapid parasite clearance and resistance mitigation.
In HIV‑positive patients, treat opportunistic infections (e.g., TMP‑SMX for Pneumocystis) after confirming CD4 count.
sections.p: Management combines antimicrobial therapy, source control and supportive care, with attention to drug resistance and local formulary constraints.

b: Always ask about recent travel, animal exposure and HIV status when evaluating fever.
When Gram stain shows Gram‑negative rods in a patient with liver disease, think Klebsiella liver abscess.
In a child with sickle‑cell disease and fever, prioritize blood cultures for Salmonella.
sections.p: Key points examiners love: integration of epidemiology, bedside clues, and rational drug choice.

whenToSeekHelp: Unexplained high‑grade fever with altered mental status
Signs of septic shock (cold extremities, low BP, altered consciousness)
